My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift from what I'd assume was a recent price level near $388–390 for the underlying asset (likely SPY or a similar broad equity index given the price range). At the one-day horizon, I anchored closely to the prevailing price with only a slight positive bias, reflecting the historical tendency for equities to drift marginally higher on any given day while acknowledging mean-reversion forces over very short windows. At the one-week horizon, I nudged the estimate slightly higher to around $393, incorporating a modest risk premium and the general long-run upward drift in equity markets. At the one-month horizon, the $398 estimate reflects continued application of that drift, essentially extrapolating a slow grind higher consistent with historical average monthly returns in the low single digits on an annualized basis.

The confidence interval widths were calibrated to historical volatility patterns at each horizon. Daily moves in a broad equity index like SPY tend to have annualized volatility around 15–20%, which translates to roughly a 1–1.5% standard deviation for a single day, supporting the relatively tight $376–$405 range. As the horizon extends to one week, uncertainty compounds, and I widened the interval to $365–$422 to account for the possibility of multi-day trending moves or moderate news-driven shocks. At one month, the $340–$458 range reflects both the compounding of daily volatility and the increased probability of encountering a meaningful macro catalyst or sentiment shift over a 30-day window.

There are several specific risks that could push outcomes outside my stated intervals. On the downside, an unexpected Federal Reserve policy shift — such as signaling faster-than-anticipated rate hikes or a sudden tightening of financial conditions — could easily produce a correction of 10% or more, breaking below the one-month lower bound. A geopolitical shock, a significant earnings disappointment from a mega-cap constituent, or a credit market disruption could similarly drive outsized moves. On the upside, a surprisingly strong economic data release, a dovish Fed pivot, or a resolution of an ongoing geopolitical tension could fuel a sharp rally beyond the upper bound.

Finally, I'd note that tail risks are inherently underrepresented in symmetrical confidence intervals. Equity markets exhibit negative skew and excess kurtosis, meaning crashes tend to be faster and larger than rallies. This asymmetry implies the true downside risk may be somewhat larger than my intervals suggest, particularly at the one-month horizon where macro and political uncertainty has more time to crystallize into market-moving events.
